result:
There's a strange kind of permission in being told you have 1000 words. Not 500, not 2000, just 1000. Enough to wander but not enough to build a city. Enough to say something real and still have room to turn around.

I wake up and the first thing I notice is the light coming through the blinds in thin, horizontal bars. It makes stripes on the ceiling and on the wall where the cat is sleeping. I don't get up right away. I lie there and listen to the house settle. The radiator ticks. Somewhere downstairs the refrigerator hums its low, constant note. My phone is on the nightstand, face down, and I leave it there. 

I think about how much of the day is spent waiting for the next thing to happen. The kettle to boil. The email to come back. The person to text first. We fill the waiting with small rituals. I make coffee the same way every morning because I like the repetition. Grind, water, wait four minutes. The smell fills the kitchen and for a few minutes the apartment feels lived in, not just occupied.

Words come easier in the morning, before I've decided what to think about. Later in the day they get filtered. You edit yourself in real time. You think, is this too much, is this too little, will they misunderstand. In the morning you can still say: the sky was the color of a faded Polaroid. That's enough.

I like walking without a destination. I like noticing how people hold their coffee cups. Some people cradle them with both hands like a small animal. Some people hold them by the lid, one finger through the hole, like it's a leash. The city is full of these tiny private languages.

I was thinking about memory the other day. How it isn't a library, it's more like a room where things keep moving. You think you put the vase on the left shelf, and now it's on the right. You swear you heard that song in 2012, and then you find out it came out in 2017. Memory edits itself to make a better story. Maybe that's why we write. To pin something down before it drifts.

There are days when I feel too much like an observer. I watch my own life from a little distance, like I'm narrating it for someone else. I catch myself thinking, this would be a good line. Then I feel guilty for thinking that, as if experiencing a moment and wanting to keep it are mutually exclusive. They aren't. The desire to remember is a form of attention.

I think about the people I have lost track of. Not lost in a dramatic way. Just slowly, through no fault of either of us. Life gets busy. Phones change. Cities change. You both keep moving forward on parallel tracks that don't intersect anymore. I wonder if they think about me the way I think about them, in brief flashes when a song comes on or a street looks like one they used to walk. Probably not. Probably yes. Both are true.

There's a comfort in small, repeatable kindnesses. The barista who remembers how I take my coffee. The neighbor who always holds the elevator. The friend who texts "how was your day?" and actually waits for the answer. We are starved for small, consistent things.

I worry sometimes about becoming cynical. It's easy to do. You see enough bad headlines, enough careless words, enough people pretending to be fine, and you start to assume the worst. Then you have to work hard to notice the good again. You have to practice looking for it.

Art helps. Not always the big art. Sometimes it's a photograph of a dog in the rain. A sentence on a bus ad. A song lyric you didn't expect to need that day. It reminds you that someone else felt something similar and bothered to shape it into something you could find.

I don't know what I want to say with these 1000 words. Maybe that's the point. Maybe you don't get to know in advance. You just start and you follow the thread until it frays or until you run out of room. I could talk about the way rain sounds different on a tin roof versus asphalt. I could talk about my grandmother's hands, how they were always slightly stained from working in the garden. I could talk about the fear of sending a text and the relief when it is received.

Time feels both too fast and too slow. The week disappears and then a single afternoon stretches out forever. I think about aging, not in a morbid way, but in the way you notice new lines on your face and realize they are a map of all the things you have done. Every smile, every frown, every squint at a bright screen. We carry our histories in our skin.

I want to be kinder to myself. I say that a lot. I also want to be less afraid of being boring. Not everyone needs to be interesting all the time. Sometimes it's enough to be present. To listen. To make tea. To say, I don't know, let's figure it out together.

The cat is up now. She stretches, yawns, and pads over to me. She doesn't care about my word count. She cares about the warm spot on my chest and the rhythm of my breathing. She is a good editor. She will walk across the keyboard if I'm being pretentious. 

If I had to summarize this whole wandering, it would be this: I am here. I am trying. I notice things. I love people, sometimes too much and sometimes not enough. I want to leave things a little better than I found them, even if it's just a clean kitchen or a kind text or a sentence that makes someone feel less alone for a second.

That's probably enough. 1000 words is a lot and also not a lot. It's a room you can walk around in. You can sit in the corner and think, you can open the window, you can leave the door ajar. I think I'm going to leave it ajar.
